title: Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing decimals

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: What is zero point four times zero point six, Champ?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Four times six is twenty-four. So, two point four?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Both numbers are less than one. Could a part of a part cover more than two whole squares?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: This square has sides of one unit. Its area is one square unit. We will call that one whole.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Cut the width into ten equal parts. Each column is one tenth of the whole.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Cut the height into ten equal parts too. Ten rows of ten make one hundred little squares.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Each little square is one hundredth of the whole.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: First, shade six tenths of the whole square. Six columns, the full height.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Multiplying by four tenths means taking four tenths of this blue area. Keep its width, and take only four of its ten rows.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One row. Two rows. Three rows. Four rows.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Four rows of six little squares. Twenty-four squares, and every square is a hundredth.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Twenty-four hundredths! Zero point two four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Yes. Taking four tenths of six tenths makes less than six tenths. Multiplication by a number between zero and one makes a positive amount smaller.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Lift out one of those hundredths. Let's look closely at its two sides.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Look closely at just one little square. Its width is one tenth, and its height is one tenth.

do.text: What is one little square worth?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One tenth of one tenth is one hundredth. That is why the product counts hundredths.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Four times six counts the pieces. Tenths times tenths names their size.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Exactly. Count the pieces, then name their size.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Bigger numbers use the same idea. Six point six times five point seven. Estimate first: about seven times six, or forty-two.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The six by five part already has area thirty. The extra strips make the total a little larger.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Six point six is sixty-six tenths. Five point seven is fifty-seven tenths.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Multiply the counts. Sixty-six times fifty is three thousand three hundred. Sixty-six times seven is four hundred sixty-two.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Add the two parts: three thousand seven hundred sixty-two. Since tenths times tenths make hundredths, that is thirty-seven point six two.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Close to forty-two, and more than thirty. The size makes sense.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The shortcut counts decimal places: digits after each point. One plus one gives two places in the product, because we divided by ten twice.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Keep placeholder zeros when needed: two tenths times five tenths is ten hundredths. Zero point one zero is the same as zero point one.

do.text: A zero can hold a place

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: For addition, ask a different question: which pieces can combine? Try two point five plus one point two five.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: If I line up the last digits, I get one point five zero.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: That arrangement puts five tenths over five hundredths. They are different-sized pieces. And the total cannot be less than two point five.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Slide two point five left until the decimal points line up. Ones over ones. Tenths over tenths.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: We can write a zero in the hundredths place. Two point five zero is exactly two point five.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Zero plus five gives five hundredths. Five plus two gives seven tenths. Two plus one gives three ones.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Three point seven five. Lining up the points keeps the units together.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Add nine point one two and four point four nine. We may need to trade.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Here are their decimal parts together: five tenths, and eleven hundredths. Two hundredths plus nine hundredths is eleven hundredths.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Trade ten of those hundredths for one tenth. Leave one hundredth behind.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The carried one means one tenth. Add it to one tenth and four tenths: six tenths.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Nine ones plus four ones makes thirteen ones. Write three ones and carry one ten.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One ten. The sum is thirteen point six one.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Five minus one point three seven. Write five as five point zero zero.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: We need hundredths to take away, but we have only whole squares. Trade one whole for ten tenths.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Then trade one of those tenths for ten hundredths.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Four wholes, nine tenths, ten hundredths. The pieces changed, but the amount is still five.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Ten hundredths minus seven leaves three hundredths.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Nine tenths minus three leaves six tenths. Four ones minus one leaves three ones.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Three point six three. I can add back one point three seven to check that I get five.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Division can find a missing side. This rectangle has area one point five square units and width five units. What is its height?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Split it into five columns, each one unit wide. Share the area equally among them.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One point five is fifteen tenths. Fifteen tenths shared among five columns gives three tenths in each.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Each column is one unit wide. So its area of three tenths means its height is three tenths too.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Check with multiplication. Five times zero point three equals one point five.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: For hundredths, share hundredths. One point seven five divided by seven means sharing one hundred seventy-five hundredths.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One hundred seventy-five divided by seven is twenty-five. Twenty-five hundredths is zero point two five.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: What if the divisor is a decimal? Return to our twenty-four hundredths. The width is six tenths. What height makes this area?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: There are six little squares across. Twenty-four squares divided into rows of six makes four rows. Each row is one tenth tall.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Four tenths! So zero point two four divided by zero point six is zero point four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Check the missing side: six tenths times four tenths gives twenty-four hundredths.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Choose the equation and its reason together. Division finds a missing side. Multiplication combines side lengths.

do.text: Match the equation AND its reason.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A written shortcut uses equal scaling. Multiply both numbers in a division by ten, and the answer stays the same.

do.text: Scale both numbers by the same amount.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Ten times as much, in groups ten times as large, gives the same number of groups.

do.text: 10 times the size of each group

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Try one point seven four divided by eight point seven. Multiply both by ten.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: That gives seventeen point four divided by eighty-seven.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Eighty-seven times two is one hundred seventy-four, so eighty-seven times two tenths is seventeen point four. The answer is zero point two.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Four friends each buy a ticket for seven dollars twenty-five cents and a drink for one dollar seventy-five cents. What do all four pay?

do.text: 4 friends. Each buys a ticket and a drink.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Cents are hundredths of a dollar. Seventy-five cents joins twenty-five cents to make another dollar. One friend pays nine dollars.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Copy the whole pair for each friend. Two pairs. Three pairs. Four pairs.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Four times nine is thirty-six dollars.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Or count all the tickets first. Four times seven point two five is twenty-nine dollars. Four drinks cost seven dollars. Add them: thirty-six.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Adding each pair, then multiplying, gives the same total as multiplying each price, then adding.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: But suppose only two friends buy drinks. Then there are four tickets and just two drinks.

do.text: 4 tickets, 2 drinks. What is the total?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Use each item's own count. Four tickets cost twenty-nine dollars. Two drinks cost three dollars fifty cents. The total is thirty-two dollars fifty cents.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Back to our little rectangle. Four rows of six, counting hundredths. Twenty-four hundredths.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Add and subtract like with like. Divide by sharing units, or finding a missing side.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A tenth of a tenth is a hundredth. Estimate first, so the decimal point lands where the size makes sense.
